source: Klinzing, Niethard, Born (2019) Mechanisms of systems memory consolidation during sleep (updates Diekelmann and Born 2010)
finding: Updated statement of active systems consolidation: repeated hippocampal replay in slow-wave sleep gradually transforms and integrates traces in neocortex, embedded in global synaptic downscaling.
numbers: Three features: replay of episodic aspects drives consolidation of hippocampus-dependent and independent memory; SWS and REM oscillations regulate information flow and local plasticity; memories become abstracted, gist-like. About 915 citations (Europe PMC).
quote: Repeated neuronal replay of representations originating from the hippocampus during slow-wave sleep leads to a gradual transformation and integration
limits: Abstract page only; no experimental numbers.
agent_relevance: Core claim for an offline agent job: replay many episodes and store abstracted gist, not just copies.

source: Marshall, Helgadottir, Molle, Born (2006) Boosting slow oscillations during sleep potentiates memory
finding: Transcranial 0.75 Hz oscillating potentials in early nocturnal NREM sleep raised slow oscillations, slow spindle activity and retention of hippocampus-dependent declarative memory. 5 Hz stimulation lowered slow oscillations and left memory unchanged.
numbers: Abstract gives no sample size or effect size. About 1342 citations.
quote: Our findings indicate that endogenous slow potential oscillations have a causal role in the sleep-associated consolidation of memory
limits: Abstract only. Later closed-loop work failed to replicate memory gains (see a11).
agent_relevance: Causal evidence that the slow-oscillation rhythm matters; a pass has to be structured, not just run.

source: Rasch, Buchel, Gais, Born (2007) Odor cues during slow-wave sleep prompt declarative memory consolidation
finding: Odor present at learning and re-presented in SWS improved retention of hippocampus-dependent declarative memory, not procedural memory. Ineffective in REM, in wake, or if the odor was absent at learning. fMRI showed hippocampal activation to the odor in SWS.
numbers: Cell sizes not read. About 841 citations.
quote: Re-exposure to the odor during slow-wave sleep (SWS) improved the retention of hippocampus-dependent declarative memories
limits: Abstract only. Cue must have been paired at learning; stage specific.
agent_relevance: Cue-triggered replay works only for cues tied to the original episode: index episodes by their context cues.

source: Wilson and McNaughton (1994) Reactivation of hippocampal ensemble memories during sleep
finding: In 3 rats, place cells that fired together during a spatial task fired together more in later slow-wave sleep than in sleep before the task. Cells inactive or with non-overlapping fields did not show this. The effect declined over the post-task sleep session.
numbers: 3 rats; pairwise co-firing compared with pre-task sleep. About 2177 citations.
quote: Information acquired during active behavior is thus re-expressed in hippocampal circuits during sleep
limits: Abstract only. Tiny N; replicated many times since.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence that experience is replayed offline; replay fades, so run the pass soon after experience.

source: Ji and Wilson (2007) Coordinated memory replay in the visual cortex and hippocampus during sleep
finding: In rats, firing sequences from awake experience were replayed in both visual cortex and hippocampus during SWS, within frames of stepwise population activity. Replay in the two regions was coordinated for the same experience.
numbers: Numbers not read. About 1237 citations.
limits: Abstract only. Correlational: shows coordination, not that it causes consolidation.
agent_relevance: Replay is coordinated between a fast store and a slow store, the CLS picture: an episodic buffer drives a slow learner.

source: Girardeau, Benchenane, Wiener, Buzsaki, Zugaro (2009) Selective suppression of hippocampal ripples impairs spatial memory
finding: Eliminating sharp wave-ripples during post-training consolidation periods impaired performance of rats on a hippocampus-dependent spatial task.
numbers: Numbers not read. About 1199 citations.
quote: Our results provide evidence for a prominent role of hippocampal SPW-Rs in memory consolidation.
limits: Abstract only. Rats; spatial task.
agent_relevance: Causal test: remove replay events and consolidation fails. Replay does the work.

source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger, Born (2004) Sleep inspires insight
finding: After initial training on a stimulus-response task with a hidden abstract rule, more than twice as many subjects found the rule after 8 h nocturnal sleep than after nocturnal or daytime wakefulness. No sleep benefit without initial training. Reaction times slowed across sleep before insight.
numbers: Exact percentages and N not read (abstract only). About 502 citations.
quote: more than twice as many subjects gained insight into the hidden rule after sleep as after wakefulness
limits: Abstract only. Independent replications are mixed and outside this angle.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the schema purpose: an offline pass over trained episodes can surface a hidden rule not found online.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex
finding: Formal model: hippocampus learns new items fast; neocortex learns slowly. Reinstatement of hippocampal memories interleaves new items with old ones so a slow connectionist network learns structure without catastrophic interference.
numbers: Connectionist simulations. About 2864 citations.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Computational reason for an offline job: interleave new episodes with old ones, do not just append.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, Lampinen (2020) Integration of new information in memory: new insights from a complementary learning systems perspective
finding: Deep linear network analysis: the part of a new item that fits known dimensions can be learned fast without interleaving. The part needing a new dimension needs gradual interleaved learning. If a new item overlaps one branch only, interleaving can focus on that branch.
numbers: Analytic and simulation work; no human data.
limits: Abstract only. Updates CLS to explain fast integration of schema-consistent information.
agent_relevance: Tells the offline job what to replay: items near the new one; schema-consistent facts can go in fast.

source: Ngo, Martinetz, Born, Molle (2013) Auditory closed-loop stimulation of the sleep slow oscillation enhances memory
finding: Auditory clicks in phase with slow-oscillation up states boosted slow oscillations, phase-coupled spindles and declarative memory consolidation. Out-of-phase stimulation was ineffective.
numbers: Numbers not read. About 690 citations.
limits: Abstract only. Not replicated by Henin 2019 in a nap and in a word-pair replication (see a11).
agent_relevance: Timing relative to the rhythm matters; gate the replay to a good moment.

source: Henin et al. (2019) Closed-loop acoustic stimulation enhances sleep oscillations but not memory performance
finding: Failed replication. Stimulation raised slow oscillation and spindle activity, but memory did not differ from sham in a VR navigation task (n=12) or a word-pair replication (n=19, double blind).
numbers: Exp 1 n=12 nap crossover; Exp 2 n=19. Bayes factors for stim=sham: Exp1 word pairs 0.302, VR speed 0.299; Exp2 0.249 (all favour the null). Recall 45-48% before and after nap in Exp 1; Exp 2 33% before, 53% after sleep.
quote: enhancement of sleep oscillations may be insufficient to enhance memory performance
limits: Small samples; nap in Exp 1 versus night in the original. Authors list possible explanations.
agent_relevance: Oscillation markers can rise without memory gain: do not treat a proxy signal as proof the offline pass worked (G3).

source: Feld, Weis, Born (2016) The limited capacity of sleep-dependent memory consolidation
finding: Sleep benefit depended on load. With 40, 160 or 320 word pairs, sleep (versus sleep deprivation, tested after 36 h) improved retention at 160 pairs, p < 0.01, and the benefit vanished at 320 pairs.
numbers: Two experiments, n=101 total. In the sleep group, retention at 320 pairs was lower than at 160 pairs.
quote: this effect completely vanished for the 320 word-pair condition
limits: Wake group slept on a recovery night before testing. Word pairs only; between-subject. Authors suggest heavy load makes sleep favour forgetting.
agent_relevance: Offline consolidation has a capacity limit: cap batch size per pass and prune, do not keep everything.

source: Lutz et al. (2026) Long-term visual gist abstraction independent of post-encoding sleep
finding: Failed replication of the authors' own earlier finding. Visual DRM gist memory persisted to 1 year, but sleeping or staying awake in the first 12 h after encoding did not change gist.
numbers: N=16, within-subject; tests immediately, at 1 week and at 1 year. High false recognition of the unseen prototype at all points.
quote: sleep effects on this process are highly dependent on task demands
limits: Small N. Authors say changed task demands made item and gist traces less distinct.
agent_relevance: Gist abstraction can happen without a sleep-like pass; sleep's role in schema formation is boundary-dependent.

source: Newbury and Monaghan (2019) When does sleep affect veridical and false memory consolidation? A meta-analysis
finding: In the DRM paradigm there was no overall effect of sleep on accurate or false memories. Effects depended on list length and on recall versus recognition testing (larger for recall).
numbers: Six moderators tested: recall/recognition, words per list, number of lists, modality, emotionality, nap/overnight.
quote: whereas there was no overall effect of sleep on either accurate or false memories
limits: Only DRM studies; gist or false memory is one proxy for schema formation.
agent_relevance: Schema-like transformation by sleep is not a general result; it is conditional on task features.

source: Ng, Noh, Spencer (2025) Does slow oscillation-spindle coupling contribute to sleep-dependent memory consolidation? A Bayesian meta-analysis (eLife)
finding: Across 23 studies and 297 effect sizes, precise and strong coupling of slow oscillations with fast spindles in the frontal lobe predicts memory consolidation. Strength depends on memory type, aging, spindle frequency and topography.
numbers: 23 studies, 297 effect sizes, four coupling measures. Strongest pooled correlation at frontal electrodes (k=29); central minus frontal rz -0.08, BF10=13.58.
quote: SO-fast SP coupling should be considered as a general physiological mechanism for memory consolidation.
limits: Correlational across individuals. Earlier literature inconsistent; authors built a new circular-linear effect size method.
agent_relevance: Mechanistic support for the oscillation hand-off, only as a correlate; no direct design lesson.

source: Ngo, Fell, Staresina (2020) Sleep spindles mediate hippocampal-neocortical coupling during long-duration ripples
finding: In epilepsy patients, spindle power rose together in hippocampus and neocortex around hippocampal ripples. Coupling was stronger for long-duration ripples. Directionality analysis pointed from neocortex to hippocampus.
numbers: 14 pre-surgical patients; 17,174 neocortical spindles, 14,748 hippocampal spindles, 3,748 hippocampal ripples.
quote: a neocortical-hippocampal-neocortical reactivation loop initiated by the neocortex
limits: Patients with epilepsy; no memory test in this analysis.
agent_relevance: Suggests the cortex starts the loop (cortical gist cues the episode): consolidation as query-driven retrieval.

source: Tononi and Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (synaptic homeostasis hypothesis)
finding: Competing account: wake strengthens synapses broadly; sleep renormalises net synaptic strength, and activity-dependent down-selection explains memory benefits rather than replay-driven strengthening.
numbers: About 1667 citations.
quote: Sleep is the price the brain pays for plasticity.
limits: Abstract only. Klinzing 2019 merges both: active consolidation embedded in global downscaling.
agent_relevance: The pruning half: an offline job should also weaken or drop weak items, not only add rules.

source: Norimoto et al. (2018) Hippocampal ripples down-regulate synapses
finding: In mice, sharp-wave ripples triggered long-lasting synaptic depression. Silencing ripples in slow-wave states prevented spontaneous downregulation of net synaptic weights and impaired learning of new memories.
numbers: Numbers not read. About 205 citations.
limits: Abstract only. Mouse.
agent_relevance: Ripple replay can prune as well as strengthen: replay as a selection step.

source: Tadros, Krishnan, Ramyaa, Bazhenov (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks (Nature Communications)
finding: A sleep-like phase (offline, local Hebbian rules, noisy input, no stored data) recovered old tasks in sequentially trained networks, and helped further when added to rehearsal.
numbers: Test accuracy %, sequential vs SRC: incremental MNIST 19.49 vs 48.47; Fashion MNIST 19.67 vs 41.68; multi-modal MNIST 47.18 vs 61.33; CIFAR10 19.01 vs 44.55. Rehearsal (0.75% old data) MNIST 79.91, with SRC 86.47; CIFAR10 39.39 vs 58.24. EWC MNIST 20.37; OWM 77.04; parallel training 98.02.
limits: Small networks (mostly two hidden layers). SRC alone is below OWM on MNIST (48.47 vs 77.04). Not a language model.
agent_relevance: An offline phase adds most on top of a stored rehearsal buffer; gains alone are partial.

source: Tadros et al. (2022), same paper: CUB-200 and trade-off
finding: During the sleep phase old-task activity and representational sparseness rose while new-task activity fell, so restoring old tasks costs some new-task accuracy.
numbers: CUB-200 (2 tasks), accuracy as old,new: sequential 5.32,95.41; SRC 63.2,45.4; rehearsal+SRC 56.55,38.05.
limits: Column pair order read as task 1, task 2 from the table. Single dataset.
agent_relevance: Consolidation trades plasticity for stability; expect some loss on the newest item.

source: Feld, Bernard, Rawson, Spiers (2022) Sleep targets highly connected global and local nodes to aid consolidation of learned graph networks
finding: Sleep (night versus day wake, within-subject) improved retention of a learned graph of 27 planets and 36 teleporters, and the benefit grew with how connected a node was.
numbers: 25 male participants recruited, df=18 so 19 analysed. Overall sleep retention t(18)=2.13, p=0.048. Degree centrality F(1,18)=4.71, p=0.044; slope with centrality F=8.26, p=0.015. Distance 4 only: t(18)=2.29, p=0.035; distances 1-3 not significant (p=0.188 to 0.327).
limits: Males only, small N, p values near 0.05.
agent_relevance: Suggests prioritising hub items in an offline pass.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Slow-wave sleep and REM sleep differentially contribute to memory representational transformation (Communications Biology)
finding: With targeted memory reactivation in overnight sleep, item-level representations were reduced while category-level representations were preserved. Higher REM to SWS ratio predicted more item-level reduction and category-level gain. SWS slow-oscillation power (1-1.25 Hz) showed the opposite pattern.
numbers: 35 participants analysed (26 female, mean age 22). REM theta (4-7 Hz) and beta (15-25 Hz) power positively linked with transformation.
limits: Correlational across individuals. Challenges a pure SWS-drives-abstraction story.
agent_relevance: Abstraction may need a second, REM-like recombination pass besides SWS-like replay.

source: Sleep deprivation meta-analyses (2022): total sleep deprivation before and after learning
finding: Total sleep deprivation after learning impairs memory with a small effect; before learning the effect is larger. Immediate tests and procedural tasks show larger effects than tests after recovery sleep and declarative tasks.
numbers: After learning Hedges g=0.277, 95% CI [0.177, 0.377]. Before learning g=0.621, 95% CI [0.473, 0.769]. Studies 1970 to 2020.
quote: Statistical power was very low in most of the analyzed studies.
limits: Egger tests show publication bias in both. Authors call for preregistered high-power replications.
agent_relevance: The post-learning consolidation effect is real but modest and possibly inflated; expect small, measurable gains.

source: Rasch and Born (2013) About sleep's role in memory (Physiological Reviews)
finding: Major review of active consolidation, passive protection from interference, and synaptic homeostasis. Full text could not be opened this session (PMC blocked, Europe PMC returned 500).
numbers: About 2783 citations (OpenAlex).
limits: Listed for follow-up; no content read, nothing here is a claim from it.
agent_relevance: Pointer for later reading only.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis, McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? Complementary learning systems theory updated
finding: CLS update for AI: fast episodic store plus slow structured learner, with replay of the store training the slow learner. Known from the search record only; text not opened.
numbers: About 345 citations (Europe PMC).
limits: Not opened; PMID given from memory and unverified.
agent_relevance: Blueprint for the agent: an episodic store replayed to train a slow rule store.
